newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait could pump back $2 bln in London stocks.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait could pump back $2 bln in London stocks.

text.p: Kuwait is expected to invest most of the $2 billion earned from its sale of British Petroleum shares in London listed firms, industry executives said on Tuesday.

But the oil-rich state, a major international investor, is expected to hold on to its remaining 6.3 percent stake in BP, with no plans to consider further sales arising over the next 12 months, they added.
"BP is aware that (Kuwait) plans to keep its 6.3 percent stake for the foreseeable future...at least for another 12 months," said a source familiar with the holding.
Dividends and capital growth boosted the value of Kuwait's BP equity investment by $1.8 billion in 1996, oil industry executives earlier told Reuters.
On Thursday Kuwait completed the world's biggest sale of a single block of shares, disposing of 170 million BP shares for 1.22 billion pounds ($2 billion).

Kuwait's foreign investment nest egg is currently valued at over $40 billion. It fell to about $35 billion from over $100 billion after the tiny state paid huge 1991 Gulf War costs and reconstruction following a seven-month Iraqi occupation.
Sources in Kuwait said the state's London-based investment arm, Kuwait Investment Office (KIO), was now aiming to reinvest the funds back in Britain in "small shares".

But the head of the state's overall investment arm Kuwait Investment Authority Ali al-Badr told Reuters on Tuesday: "The money will be reinvested...We have holdings inside and outside Britain and we buy and sell every day."
KIO had earlier described the sale as a "rebalancing exercise" as its holding became disproportionately big, adding that it will remain a "core" investor in BP in the foreseeable future.
Official sources in Kuwait said the state enjoyed sovereign immunity and was not obliged to pay taxes on the BP sale as the owner is sovereign KIO.

Kuwaiti economist Jassem al-Saadoun said Kuwait was exempted from paying taxes on the sale of BP shares when it agreed with the British government in the late 1980s to cut its holding in the oil giant to no more than 9.9 percent after rising to 22.7 percent.

"This latest sale of BP shares is within the state's general policy to diversify away from oil. Such a large holding would be in conflict with the official strategy," he added. "They do not want to put all their eggs in the same basket."
Kuwait is a major OPEC producer with a two million barrel per day (bpd) output and wide refining holdings both at home and abroad.
Kuwait has also started steps to sell its wholly-owned Santa Fe International Corp which was acquired in 1981.
"The Santa Fe situation is more complicated than BP. Santa Fe has resulted in large losses and Kuwait is trying to sell it off to correct a bad situation," Saadoun said.
